newsitem.title: USA: McVeigh faces battle for life after bomb verdict.
newsitem.headline: McVeigh faces battle for life after bomb verdict.

text.p: Timothy McVeigh faced a life-and-death battle on Tuesday after a jury found him guilty of blowing up the Oklahoma City federal building, killing 168 people in one of the blackest chapters in U.S. history.

McVeigh, 29, who once fought for his country in the Gulf War, was convicted on Monday of using a huge truck bomb to destroy a symbol of the U.S. government, the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City, on April 19, 1995.

On Wednesday, a second phase of the trial will begin at which the same jury will hear testimony on whether McVeigh deserves death by lethal injection or life imprisonment as punishment for a crime that outraged and horrified Americans.

"Given the current climate surrounding the case ... it's hard to imagine he's going to escape the death penalty," said Robert Precht, director of the office of public service at the University of Michigan Law School.

Relatives of bombing victims wept in the crowded Denver courtroom as federal Judge Richard Matsch read the verdict reached by seven men and five women jurors after deliberating for 23 hours over four days.
In both Denver and Oklahoma City, the verdict was greeted with joy, relief and tears by survivors and victims' relatives, most of whom were convinced of McVeigh's guilt.

"Just to hear that one word -- guilty -- on all 11 counts. It was just such a relief," said Marsha Kight, whose daughter, 23-year-old Frankie Merrell, was killed in the bombing. "The tears came, tears of relief that this chapter is closed."

In Oklahoma City, hundreds of people who had gathered at the bombing site applauded and punched the air in triumph. "I am sure there are 168 people who are smiling down on us from above," said Dan McKinney, whose wife Linda died in the bombing.
But for many survivors, the joy of winning a conviction could not wipe out the pain of their loss.
Outside the tightly-guarded Denver courthouse, hundreds of people, many of them federal office workers, gathered quickly after the verdict to cheer the prosecution team led by Joe Hartzler.
Elsewhere in the United States, there was applause and demands for vengeance but little surprise at the news.
"This is a very important and long overdue day for the survivors and families of those who died in Oklahoma City," President Bill Clinton said.

McVeigh, who did not testify in his defence, kept his eyes fixed on Matsch as the judge read the verdict. Afterward, he betrayed no emotion as he shook hands solemnly with chief defence attorney Stephen Jones.

The fertiliser and fuel oil bomb brought nine stories of the concrete building crashing down, trapping and crushing office workers, federal employees and 19 children, many of whom were in a day care centre in the building.

Prosecutors said McVeigh was a right-wing fanatic who carried out the attack to avenge 80 Branch Davidian cult members killed in a confrontation with federal agents at Waco, Texas exactly two years earlier.
The prosecution, which presented a wealth of circumstantial evidence tying McVeigh to the bombing, said he wanted to see "blood flow in the streets of America."

Defence lawyers attacked prosecution evidence and suggested the real bomber may have died in the blast, but legal analysts said they failed to give a credible explanation for McVeigh's movements around the time of the bombing if he was not involved.

The prosecution and defence each have a chance to call more witnesses during the penalty phase, expected to last about a week. Prosecutors are expected to call 40 or 50 witnesses, many of them survivors and relatives of victims who will give heart-rending testimony about their suffering.

Defence lawyers are expected to call witnesses who will testify about McVeigh's good Army record and family background. The jury will then decide if the aggravating factors outweigh the mitigating ones and whether McVeigh should be put to death.
Precht said the defence may say McVeigh is "suffering from a severe disturbance, perhaps stemming from his Gulf War days" that interfered with his ability to tell right from wrong.

The jury found McVeigh guilty of conspiracy, two bombing charges and eight counts of first-degree murder for eight federal law enforcement agents killed in the blast. Oklahoma authorities now plan to file state murder charges on behalf of the 160 other victims.

On Tuesday, Matsch will hear legal motions on how the penalty phase will be conducted. Tuesday's hearing will be outside the presence of jurors, who were allowed to return home on Monday after being sequestered during their deliberations.
